title: Voting Ensemble - Hard and Soft
abstract:
The simplest ensemble. Train several different algorithms on the
full dataset and combine their answers — by majority vote for
classification, by mean for regression. This document covers the mechanism, the
two assumptions the notes state (all models different, all better than 50%), the
distinction between hard voting on labels and soft voting on probabilities, why
soft voting usually wins, weighted voting, and how a voting ensemble differs from
bagging.

blocks.t: The Mechanism
From the notes

Every model is trained on the full data. Each predicts on the testing
data point $X_q$, and the answers are combined by majority voting.
Assumptions:

This is classification. In case of regression, we take the mean of the
3 predictions.

blocks.cap:
The notes' diagram. Note that every model receives the full
 data — this is what distinguishes voting from bagging, where each model gets
 a different bootstrap sample.

blocks.t: Where the diversity comes from

Since all models see identical data, the only remaining source of diversity is
the algorithm itself. A voting ensemble therefore combines
different kinds of model — logistic regression, KNN, a decision tree,
Naive Bayes — each of which makes different assumptions and therefore different
mistakes.

This is the direct answer to Topic 58's requirement that base models be
different. Voting three identical logistic regressions gives $\rho=1$ and no
benefit whatsoever.
Why the two assumptions are exactly the right ones

They are the two conditions of Condorcet's theorem (Topic 58).
All models different makes the errors close to independent, so they cancel
rather than compound. All accuracy $>50\%$ makes each vote informative —
below that threshold the theorem runs in reverse and more models make the
ensemble worse.
Hard and Soft Voting
From the notes

items:
Classification — the class with the most
 votes wins. Regression — we take the average of the
 predictions.

Classification — each model predicts a
 class probability instead of a label, and the probabilities for
 each class are averaged.

blocks.cap:
The notes' spam example. Hard voting counts labels; soft voting
 averages probabilities. Here both give "spam", but they need not.

blocks.t: The notes' arithmetic
Three models predict $P(\text{spam})$ of $0.7$, $0.4$ and $0.8$.

\text{Spam Prob}=\frac{0.7+0.4+0.8}{3}=0.63,
 \qquad
 \text{Not Spam Prob}=\frac{0.3+0.6+0.2}{3}=0.37
The averaged probabilities sum to 1, and the higher one wins. Formally:

\text{hard: } \hat y=\text{mode}{\hat y_1,\ldots,\hat y_M},
 \qquad
 \text{soft: } \hat y=\arg\max_c \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} P_m(c\mid x) .
Why soft voting usually wins

Hard voting discards the models' confidence. Consider three models predicting
$P(\text{spam})$ of $0.49$, $0.49$ and $0.99$:

items:
Hard: votes are not-spam, not-spam, spam $\Rightarrow$
 not spam, 2–1.

blocks.t:
Two models were barely uncertain; one was almost certain. Soft voting lets the
confident model outweigh two hesitant ones, which is usually the better decision
— and it also produces a probability you can threshold (Topic 53), where hard
voting yields only a label.
Soft voting requires calibrated probabilities

Averaging probabilities is only meaningful if they mean the same thing across
models — and they often do not. Naive Bayes is notoriously over-confident,
routinely outputting $0.999$; an unpruned decision tree outputs exactly $0$ or
$1$ from pure leaves. Averaging those with a well-calibrated logistic regression
lets the over-confident model dominate.

Fixes: wrap poorly calibrated models in CalibratedClassifierCV, or use
hard voting, or weight the models explicitly.
Weighted Voting
Not every model deserves an equal say. Both variants accept weights:
\text{soft: } \hat y=\arg\max_c \frac{\sum_m w_m P_m(c\mid x)}{\sum_m w_m}

Reasonable choices are validation accuracy, or weights tuned by grid search.
Note that this is the point at which voting starts to resemble stacking
(Topic 70) — except that stacking learns the combination rather than
having you specify it.

blocks.cap:
Left: four different base models and the two voting ensembles. The
 ensemble beats every individual member. Right: majority-vote accuracy against
 individual accuracy, showing why the $>50\%$ assumption matters.

blocks.t: Voting vs Bagging
Its practical niche

Voting is the ensemble you reach for when you already have several tuned models
of different kinds and want a cheap combination. It is rarely the best ensemble
— bagging and boosting usually beat it — but it is the easiest to build, needs
no new hyperparameters, and reliably improves on its own best member.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import VotingClassifier, VotingRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier, KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 10))
y = (X[:, 0] + .8*X[:, 1] - .5*X[:, 2] + .4*X[:, 0]*X[:, 1]
     + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. FOUR DIFFERENT ALGORITHMS, ALL ON THE FULL DATA
# =====================================================================
base = [
    ("lr",  make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))),
    ("knn", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(25))),
    ("dt",  DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=6, random_state=0)),
    ("nb",  GaussianNB()),
]
print(f"{'model':6s} {'cv accuracy':>12s}")
for name, m in base:
    print(f"{name:6s} {cross_val_score(m, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean():12.4f}")
# All four are > 50% -- the notes' second assumption.

hard = VotingClassifier(base, voting="hard").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
soft = VotingClassifier(base, voting="soft").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\n{'HARD voting':16s} test {hard.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"{'SOFT voting':16s} test {soft.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"{'best single':16s} test "
      f"{max(m.fit(X_tr,y_tr).score(X_te,y_te) for _, m in base):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 2. HARD VOTING, BY HAND
# =====================================================================
preds = np.array([m.fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te) for _, m in base])
majority = (preds.mean(axis=0) >= 0.5).astype(int)
print(f"\nmanual majority == sklearn hard: "
      f"{np.array_equal(majority, hard.predict(X_te))}")

print(f"\n{'':16s} " + "".join(f"{n_:>6s}" for n_, _ in base) + "  vote  true")
for i in range(6):
    votes = preds[:, i]
    print(f"row {i:<12d} " + "".join(f"{v:6d}" for v in votes) +
          f" {int(votes.mean() >= .5):6d} {y_te[i]:5d}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. SOFT VOTING, BY HAND -- the notes' arithmetic
# =====================================================================
probs = np.array([m.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1] for _, m in base])
avg = probs.mean(axis=0)
print(f"\nmanual soft == sklearn soft: "
      f"{np.array_equal((avg >= .5).astype(int), soft.predict(X_te))}")

# The notes' spam example:
p_spam = np.array([0.7, 0.4, 0.8])
print(f"\nSpam Prob     = ({'+'.join(map(str, p_spam))})/3 = {p_spam.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Not Spam Prob = ({'+'.join(map(str, 1-p_spam))})/3 = {(1-p_spam).mean():.4f}")
print(f"-> {'SPAM' if p_spam.mean() > .5 else 'NOT SPAM'}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. WHERE HARD AND SOFT DISAGREE
# =====================================================================
case = np.array([0.49, 0.49, 0.99])
print(f"\nprobabilities {case}")
print(f"  hard votes: {(case >= .5).astype(int)} -> "
      f"{'spam' if (case >= .5).mean() > .5 else 'NOT spam'}  (2-1)")
print(f"  soft mean : {case.mean():.4f} -> "
      f"{'SPAM' if case.mean() > .5 else 'not spam'}")
# Two barely-uncertain models outvote one nearly-certain one under hard
# voting. Soft voting lets confidence count.

disagree = hard.predict(X_te) != soft.predict(X_te)
print(f"\nthey disagree on {disagree.sum()} of {len(y_te)} test rows "
      f"({disagree.mean():.1%})")
if disagree.sum():
    print(f"  hard is right on {(hard.predict(X_te)[disagree] == y_te[disagree]).mean():.1%}")
    print(f"  soft is right on {(soft.predict(X_te)[disagree] == y_te[disagree]).mean():.1%}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. DIVERSITY IS THE WHOLE POINT
# =====================================================================
print(f"\npairwise disagreement between base models:")
print(f"{'':6s}" + "".join(f"{n_:>7s}" for n_, _ in base))
for (n1, _), p1 in zip(base, preds):
    print(f"{n1:6s}" + "".join(f"{(p1 != p2).mean():7.3f}" for p2 in preds))

identical = VotingClassifier(
    [(f"lr{i}", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)))
     for i in range(4)], voting="soft").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\n4 IDENTICAL models: {identical.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"1 model alone     : "
      f"{make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(X_tr,y_tr).score(X_te,y_te):.4f}")
print("-> exactly the same. rho = 1 means no benefit (Topic 58).")

# =====================================================================
# 6. SOFT VOTING NEEDS CALIBRATED PROBABILITIES
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'model':10s} {'mean P':>8s} {'frac >0.99':>11s} {'frac <0.01':>11s}")
for name, m in base:
    p = m.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    print(f"{name:10s} {p.mean():8.4f} {(p > .99).mean():11.3f} {(p < .01).mean():11.3f}")
# Naive Bayes and an unpruned tree saturate at 0 and 1 -- they DOMINATE the
# average regardless of whether they are right.

raw_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0)
cal_tree = CalibratedClassifierCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), cv=5)
for tag, m in [("uncalibrated tree", raw_tree), ("calibrated tree", cal_tree)]:
    ens = VotingClassifier(base[:3] + [("t", m)], voting="soft")
    print(f"soft voting with {tag:20s} "
          f"cv {cross_val_score(ens, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean():.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. WEIGHTED VOTING
# =====================================================================
weights = [cross_val_score(m, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean() for _, m in base]
w = np.array(weights) - 0.5                       # weight by advantage over chance
wv = VotingClassifier(base, voting="soft", weights=w).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nequal weights   test {soft.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"accuracy weights test {wv.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}   weights {w.round(3)}")

gs = GridSearchCV(VotingClassifier(base, voting="soft"),
                  {"weights": [[1,1,1,1], [2,1,1,1], [3,1,2,1], [2,2,1,1]]},
                  cv=5, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"tuned weights   test {gs.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}  {gs.best_params_}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. REGRESSION -- "we take the mean of the 3 predictions"
# =====================================================================
yr = X[:, 0]*2 + X[:, 1] - .5*X[:, 2]**2 + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
Xr_tr, Xr_te, yr_tr, yr_te = train_test_split(X, yr, test_size=.3, random_state=0)

reg_base = [
    ("ridge", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge())),
    ("knn",   make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsRegressor(20))),
    ("tree",  DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=6, random_state=0)),
]
vr = VotingRegressor(reg_base).fit(Xr_tr, yr_tr)
print(f"\n{'model':10s} {'test R2':>9s}")
for name, m in reg_base:
    print(f"{name:10s} {m.fit(Xr_tr, yr_tr).score(Xr_te, yr_te):9.4f}")
print(f"{'VOTING':10s} {vr.score(Xr_te, yr_te):9.4f}   <- the MEAN of the three")

manual = np.mean([m.predict(Xr_te) for _, m in reg_base], axis=0)
print(f"manual mean == VotingRegressor: {np.allclose(manual, vr.predict(Xr_te))}")

# =====================================================================
# 9. THE ASSUMPTION THAT ACCURACY MUST EXCEED 50%
# =====================================================================
class WorseThanChance:
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X, y); return self
    def predict(self, X):
        return 1 - self.m.predict(X)              # deliberately inverted
    def predict_proba(self, X):
        return self.m.predict_proba(X)[:, ::-1]
    def get_params(self, deep=True): return {}
    def set_params(self, **kw): return self

bad = [("lr", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))),
       ("b1", WorseThanChance()), ("b2", WorseThanChance())]
print(f"\ngood model alone            : "
      f"{make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(X_tr,y_tr).score(X_te,y_te):.4f}")
print(f"voted with 2 sub-chance models: "
      f"{VotingClassifier(bad, voting='hard').fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
# The ensemble is DRAGGED BELOW the good model. Condorcet in reverse.
Worked Examples
Hard vote and soft vote can disagree
Three classifiers estimate $P(\text{class }1)$ for the same input: $[0.9,\;0.4,\;0.45]$.
Hard voting. Each model casts a vote for its predicted class (threshold $0.5$): $[1,\,0,\,0]$. Majority: class 0 (two votes to one).
Soft voting. Average the probabilities: $\bar p = \dfrac{0.9+0.4+0.45}{3} = 0.583$. Since $0.583 > 0.5$, the prediction is class 1.

Why they disagree. One model is very confident (0.9) and the other two are only mildly against (0.4 and 0.45). Hard voting ignores confidence and counts only the 2-vs-1 tally. Soft voting lets the confident model outweigh the two lukewarm ones.

Guideline. Soft voting usually performs better when every member outputs well-calibrated probabilities. Hard voting is the fallback for models without predict_proba, such as a plain SVM without probability calibration.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
In a voting ensemble every model is trained on the full data,
 and the predictions are combined by majority voting.

Assumptions: all models are different, and all model accuracy
 $>50\%$ — the two conditions of Condorcet's theorem.

Because all models see the same data, the diversity must come from the
 algorithms: logistic regression, KNN, a tree, Naive Bayes.

Hard voting — classification: the class with the most
 votes wins; regression: the average of the predictions.

Soft voting — each model predicts a class probability
 instead of a label, and the probabilities are averaged.
 E.g. spam $=(0.7+0.4+0.8)/3=0.63$, not-spam $=0.37$.

Soft usually wins because it keeps the models' confidence: one
 certain model can outweigh two hesitant ones.

But soft voting requires calibrated probabilities — Naive Bayes
 and unpruned trees saturate at 0 and 1 and dominate the average.

Weights let better models count more, which is the step towards
 stacking (Topic 70).
In regression we take the mean of the predictions.

Voting uses different algorithms on the same data; bagging uses
 the same algorithm on different data.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Hard voting or soft voting?

Soft, when every base model produces meaningful probabilities. It preserves
confidence, so a nearly certain model can outweigh two hesitant ones, and it
yields a probability you can threshold. Use hard voting when some models have no
predict_proba, or when their probabilities are badly calibrated.
Q. Why must the base models be different?

Because the variance of an average is floored at $\rho\sigma^2$. Voting four
identical logistic regressions gives exactly the accuracy of one. In a voting
ensemble the only available source of diversity is the algorithm, since every
model sees the same data.
Q. Why must each model be better than 50%?

Condorcet's theorem cuts both ways. Above chance, adding models drives majority
accuracy towards 1; below chance, it drives it towards 0. A model worse than
random actively drags the ensemble down.

Q. What is the risk of soft voting with a Naive Bayes model in the
mix?

Naive Bayes is systematically over-confident — it routinely outputs $0.999$
because of its independence assumption. Averaged with well-calibrated models it
dominates the mean regardless of whether it is right. Calibrate it first, or use
hard voting.
Q. How does voting differ from bagging?

Voting uses different algorithms on the full dataset; bagging uses
the same algorithm on different bootstrap samples. Voting draws its
diversity from the models, bagging from the data — and bagging typically uses
hundreds of models where voting uses a handful.
Q. When would you use a voting ensemble in practice?

When you have already tuned several models of different kinds and want a cheap,
reliable improvement over the best of them. It adds almost no hyperparameters. If
you are willing to fit a meta-model to learn the combination, stacking (Topic 70)
usually does better.
